newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Outlooks the focus for Australian profit season.
newsitem.headline: Outlooks the focus for Australian profit season.

text.p: Investors will be watching keenly for signs of a pick-up in performance when the bulk of Australia's listed companies post end-of-year results in the upcoming reporting season for the period to June 30.
The market has factored in subdued results, but is expecting a strong earnings recovery among cyclical stocks in line with a more buoyant economy, say fund managers and equities strategists.
An earnings catch-up is vital to justify the strong run-up in the share price of cyclical stocks based on double digit earnings forecasts for the next two years.

"The markets will be looking for any comment management make about the next 12 months, what type of conditions they expect and also how conditions have been since year-end," said Merrill Lynch equities strategist John Banos.
"It's really the forward looking comments the market is going to latch onto, the year past will be pretty tough," Banos said.
Excluding financial stocks, Merrill Lynch is forecasting just 0.7 percent industrial sector earnings growth for the 1996/97 financial year.

The subdued 1997 reporting season, which runs until September 12 for companies whose financial year or half year ends on June 30, will be in line with the low-inflationary environment and sluggish domestic economy.

Bankers Trust Investment Bank equities strategist David Rees said he expected improvements in the retail sector, building materials, chemical and food and household sectors, though earning were growing from a low base.

The consumer sector -- alcohol and tobacco, retail, wholesale, tourism and leisure -- should see three-to-five percent earnings per share (EPS) growth, with slightly lower EPS growth for cyclical stocks.
"Those companies that will tend to do a little better will be the ones that have solid or reasonable offshore operations," said Perpetual Funds Management's head of Australian equities Peter Morgan.
The general tone of the reporting season had been factored into the market, but the outlook painted for the first quarter would be critical for many companies, Morgan said.
Some smaller companies had seen share prices run up to 14 or 15 times earnings, but most were domestically based and still having to watch costs quite closely.
BNP Investment Management fund manager Anton Tagliaferro said he expected cyclical stocks to reflect the problems of the economy during the past 12 months.
"Gaming will do well, telecommunications will do well, private health care will do well and energy will do well," Tagliaferro said.
The market could also see more profit warnings, following a number of downgrades by smaller companies in recent weeks.
"With companies exposed to the domestic economy there is still a bit of stress out there and that hasn't gone away yet," Tagliaferro said.
Banos said investors would watch the number of earnings downgrades and upgrades relative to expectations.
"In the last profit reporting season 3-6 months ago, generally earnings were a little below analysts's expectations," he said, pointing to some recent weaker economic data.
"In some cases because of the softer economy you might find there are a few disappoinments," Banos said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1871
